title: Humans Appear in AI Phone Calls: Behind a Test Meta Stopped
part1:
Making a haircut appointment, checking a store’s stock, and getting a price estimate from a business. Meta’s AI agent, Muse, can call businesses and stores in the United States.

But behind those calls, an unexpected player appeared.

For some calls made through Muse, Meta tested having trained human contract workers—not AI—make the calls and complete the conversations. They called them “human concierges.”

The important point is that this was not a case where AI spoke first and a human took over only at the end. What has been confirmed is that human contract workers handled some calls and completed the conversations.
part2:
You may think you asked AI to make a call, but a human may actually handle it. That is quite a big reveal in the world of phone calls. However, it was not enough to look only at whether the system worked well.

To move a call forward, users’ sensitive information may sometimes be needed. That information could be shared unintentionally with contract workers at a call center. Meta employees raised concerns about this privacy issue.

It has not been confirmed that a large amount of information was leaked. The problem was that Meta started a test in which human contract workers handled calls, without giving a proper explanation. Even if people think they are leaving the task to AI, if someone else is actually handling the information, that fact needs to be explained first.
part3:
A Meta executive admitted that this was a mistake. Meta then put the human concierge feature back on hold for the time being. It did not stop the phone feature as a whole. It stopped the system in which human contract workers handled the calls.

Meta says it will make the phone feature available only when preparations are complete and it can give a proper explanation. What was really at issue in AI phone calls was not just how well the calls were handled. It was whether Meta could clearly say who was on the other end of the call.
in_one_line: Meta paused its AI calling test after human contractors, not AI, handled some calls without proper disclosure.
